summaries.example: Imagine two school days. On one day, you feel cheerful but learn nothing, see no friends, and cannot do anything you care about. On the other, you work hard, learn something new, help a friend, and feel proud, even though you are tired. A philosopher might ask which day was better for you and why. Different theories of well-being may give different answers.
summaries.summary: Well-being is a philosophical name for what makes someone's life go well or badly for that person. It is wider than just health or a happy feeling. A person's well-being might involve pleasure, friendship, knowledge, meaningful activities, or other things that benefit them. Philosophers have proposed three main kinds of theory. Hedonism says that pleasure and freedom from pain are central. Desire theories say that getting what a person wants is central. Objective list theories say that some goods, such as friendship or knowledge, can benefit a person whether or not those goods are simply pleasant or desired. The entry also discusses challenges to the very idea of saying something is “good for” a person, and explains why well-being matters when we think about morality and helping others.
key_ideas: Well-being means how good or bad a life is for the person living it.
Health can be part of well-being, but well-being may also include friendship, pleasure, knowledge, and other goods.
Philosophers disagree about whether pleasure, fulfilled desires, or a wider list of goods matters most.
A person's well-being can be considered at one moment or across their whole life.
Well-being is important in ethics because people often ask what actions help or harm others.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about well-being helps us ask better questions about a good life. It reminds us that a person's health, feelings, choices, relationships, and learning may all matter. It also helps us think carefully before deciding whether an action truly helps someone. There is no single agreed answer in the entry, so the important skill is understanding the different reasons and objections.

important_terms.definition: How well a person's life is going for that person. It includes what makes the person's life better or worse for them.
Something that is valuable for a person, not merely useful for getting something else.
A view that pleasure makes life better and pain makes life worse.
A view that a person's life goes better when the things they want are fulfilled.
A view that several things, such as friendship or knowledge, can make a life better, even beyond pleasure or wishes.

questions_to_think_about: Would a fun day always be better for you than a difficult day in which you learn something important?
Can something be good for you even if you do not want it right now?
Which things would you put on a list of what helps a person live well?
Should helping other people count as good for the helper, good for others, or both?

summaries.example: Suppose a student is offered a device that will create convincing experiences of writing a prize-winning novel, having loyal friends, and accomplishing meaningful projects. The student will believe these events are real, but outside the device none of them will occur. A hedonist may judge the choice favorably if the experiences contain enough pleasure. A desire theorist may object that the student's desires to write, befriend, and accomplish are not actually fulfilled. An objective-list theorist may stress that real achievement, knowledge, or relationships matter independently of how they feel.
summaries.summary: The philosophical concept of well-being concerns what is ultimately good or bad for an individual. It is therefore distinct from moral value, aesthetic value, and short-term happiness, although these may contribute to a person's well-being. The entry examines two challenges to the concept itself. Moore argues that “my good” may collapse into either the goodness of an experience or the goodness of my having it. Scanlon questions whether the varied things that benefit people form a unified category that can guide ethical comparison. The entry then presents the standard classification of theories. Hedonism makes pleasant experience and the absence of pain fundamental. Desire theories make the fulfillment of desires fundamental, with increasingly sophisticated versions appealing to comprehensive, global, or informed desires. Objective list theories hold that goods such as knowledge, friendship, achievement, or autonomy may contribute to well-being independently of pleasure or desire. Each family faces objections, and the entry emphasizes that a theory must answer both what constitutes well-being and what makes those constituents good for the person. Finally, well-being is connected to welfarism, utilitarian moral reasoning, and the relation between virtue and a person's own good.
key_ideas: Well-being is a form of value indexed to a person: it concerns what is good or bad for that person, not simply what is morally or aesthetically good.

The concept faces challenges from G. E. Moore, who questioned whether “good for” adds anything beyond ordinary goodness, and T. M. Scanlon, who questioned whether well-being forms a unified category useful for ethics.
Hedonism identifies well-being with pleasure over pain, but the experience machine and differences between apparently higher and lower pleasures create pressure against simple versions.
Desire theories avoid some problems for hedonism, yet cases involving harmful desires, addiction, limited information, and unusual preferences create difficulties.
Objective list theories include goods not reducible to pleasure or desire-satisfaction, but they must explain what unites the list and how we can know which items belong on it.
Well-being can be assessed at a time or over a life, and theories of morality may disagree about whether well-being is the only ultimate value.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory of well-being affects how we evaluate choices, policies, and moral duties. It influences what counts as helping someone, what sacrifices are worthwhile, and whether a benefit must match the person's wishes or experiences. It also clarifies disagreements that can otherwise remain hidden: people may agree that someone should be helped while disagreeing about what help really improves that person's life. Studying these theories develops careful thinking about value, evidence, personal perspective, and moral reasoning.

important_terms.definition: The value a life has for the person whose life it is, considered as what ultimately benefits or harms that person.
Value understood as being beneficial to a particular individual, rather than value that is simply good without reference to anyone.
The position that well-being consists in an overall balance of pleasure over pain.
A theory holding that well-being increases when a person's desires or preferences are fulfilled; versions differ about which desires count.
A theory listing goods such as knowledge, friendship, achievement, or autonomy that contribute to well-being beyond mere pleasure or desire-fulfillment.
The thought experiment in which a machine supplies desired experiences while leaving open whether the person's real projects, relationships, and achievements exist.
The view that well-being is the only ultimate value, including in the explanation of moral reasons.
The distinction between identifying the constituents of well-being and explaining why those constituents are good for someone.

questions_to_think_about: If an experience machine gave you everything you valued from the inside, what might still be missing, and why?
Should an informed desire to do something unusual determine whether that activity benefits the person?
Can knowledge or friendship improve someone's life even when they do not currently want either?
Is a theory of well-being needed in order to compare present sacrifice with future benefits?
Could well-being matter morally without being the only thing that matters morally?

summaries.example: Maya wants to become a musician. Practicing is tiring, and she sometimes wishes she could stop. Still, she learns new skills, performs with friends, and reaches a goal she has cared about for years. A hedonist might ask whether the pleasure outweighs the frustration. A desire theory might focus on whether her wish to become a musician is fulfilled. An objective list theory might also count friendship, achievement, and knowledge, even if some parts of the project are not enjoyable.
summaries.summary: In philosophy, well-being means how a person's life is going for that person. It includes more than health and more than a temporary feeling of happiness. Friendship, pleasure, knowledge, achievement, and meaningful activities might all contribute, while pain and other harms can reduce well-being. The entry discusses challenges from Moore and Scanlon, who question whether “good for” is a clear or useful idea. It then compares three major theories. Hedonism says that pleasure over pain makes a life better. Desire theories say that fulfilled wants or preferences make a life better, though philosophers disagree about whether present, long-term, or fully informed desires should count. Objective list theories say that some goods belong in well-being even when they are not simply pleasant or desired. The entry also connects well-being with moral theories, especially welfarism, which treats well-being as the only ultimate value. These debates remain open because each theory explains some important cases while facing difficult objections.
key_ideas: Philosophical well-being is broader than health and is not exactly the same as feeling happy at one moment.
What is good for a person is different from what is morally good or artistically beautiful, although these kinds of value can be related.
The three familiar theories are hedonism, desire theories, and objective list theories.
Thought experiments test these theories by asking whether pleasure, desire-satisfaction, or real goods matter most.
Well-being can describe a whole life or a particular period, and philosophers debate whether the timing of good and bad experiences matters.
Well-being is important in moral philosophy because many ethical views ask how actions affect people.
summaries.why_it_matters: Ideas about well-being shape how we think about education, health, friendships, personal goals, and moral choices. They help us distinguish giving someone what they want from genuinely helping them, and they encourage us to ask whether a pleasant experience is enough for a good life. Understanding the competing theories also makes disagreements more precise: people can examine whether they disagree about the ingredients of well-being or about why those ingredients benefit someone.

important_terms.definition: How well or badly a person's life goes for that person, including benefits and harms across a life.
Value that belongs to someone’s own good, rather than value that is simply moral or beautiful.
The theory that pleasure improves well-being and pain reduces it, usually by comparing the overall balance.
The theory that well-being depends on satisfying a person's wants, preferences, or desires.
The theory that several goods, such as knowledge and friendship, make a life better, whether or not they are wanted or pleasurable.
A thought experiment about a machine that provides perfect experiences while raising doubts about whether real achievements and relationships are needed.
The view that well-being is the only ultimate kind of value.

questions_to_think_about: Would a machine-created life be as good as a real life if the experiences felt exactly the same?
Should something count as good for you if you want it only because you have been misled?
What belongs on your own objective list of goods?
Can a person’s life go well overall even if some periods are very bad?
Does doing the right thing always improve the well-being of the person who does it?
